clue.text: Comedian decapitated in obscure crime

indicators.note: the shortened comedian sits inside the word for obscure

parts.note: to obscure something is to hide it

indicators.note: a beheaded word loses its first letter, here the comedian's

parts.note: a comic is a comedian

explanation.surface: A comic without a head lies at the centre of a murky criminal case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'obscure' reads as an adjective describing the crime, but it is the verb meaning to conceal, which forms the outer part.
explanation.definitionFit: Killing a person is the gravest offence, a specific kind of crime.

clue.text: Another messenger reveals himself

indicators.note: the messenger shows himself within the words, so his name lies in their letters

explanation.surface: A second courier comes forward and shows who he is.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'anotHER MESsenger'; the messenger of the Greek gods shows himself in his own description.
explanation.definitionFit: The winged herald of the Olympian gods carried their messages.

clue.text: Badger spots old car

parts.note: moles are spots on the skin
the Model T was an old Ford car

explanation.surface: A badger notices a vintage car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badger' looks like the animal, but here it is the verb meaning to harass.
explanation.definitionFit: To badger is to pester or harass, a sense shared by this verb.

clue.text: Dealing successfully with fixing in tooth

explanation.surface: Handling a dental repair well.
explanation.definitionFit: Managing well is getting by; in dentistry it is also a thin metal cap fitted over a tooth.

clue.text: Quasimodo's identical twin?

parts.note: Quasimodo rang the bells of Notre-Dame; a lookalike twin, a perfect copy, is described by a phrase meaning a lifeless bellman

explanation.surface: Asking who the hunchback's double would be.
explanation.walkthrough: Quasimodo is the bell-ringing hunchback of Notre-Dame; the phrase for an exact double, read literally, is a bell-ringer who has died.
explanation.definitionFit: An exact lookalike is called by this idiom, and the bell-ringer pun gives the cryptic sense.

clue.text: Quiet musketeer evokes pity

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction to play quietly
Athos is one of Dumas's Three Musketeers

explanation.surface: A soft-spoken swordsman stirs up sympathy.
explanation.definitionFit: The quality in art that stirs compassion is a sense of pity or sadness.

clue.text: Lady wove fantastically, having said as much

indicators.note: done fantastically means wildly, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman wove wonderfully, as she openly claimed.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something as openly declared means by one's own admission, having stated it.

clue.text: Husband excitedly peruses the evening star

indicators.note: excitedly suggests agitation, so these letters are stirred about

explanation.surface: A husband eagerly studies Venus at dusk.
explanation.definitionFit: The classical name for Venus seen after sunset is the evening star.

clue.text: Quiet holy man's 'ale and 'earty

parts.note: ST is short for saint, a holy man
hale and hearty means fit and well, dropped Hs make the word for that lose its H

explanation.surface: A cheerful saint, in Cockney, is sound and well.
explanation.walkthrough: Hale and hearty means in good health; dropping its first H, as the apostrophes show, leaves EALTHY.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving quietly and secretly is sneaky, furtive, unnoticed.

clue.text: Loyal rep excited to take part in training

indicators.note: something excited is stirred up, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A keen sales representative is eager to join in a staff course.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting out scenarios is a common exercise in staff instruction, so to act in one is to join a training session.

clue.text: Rodent eating Sunday's dessert

indicators.note: the rodent swallows the letter, so it goes inside

parts.note: a mouse is a rodent
S is the abbreviation for Sunday

explanation.surface: A mouse nibbles at the weekend pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: A light whipped chocolate or fruit pudding is a sweet course after a meal.

clue.text: Relies on goulash in Shakespearean setting

indicators.note: a goulash is a stew, a mixed jumble, so these letters are stirred into another order

explanation.surface: A cook trusts a stew for a dramatic scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goulash' looks like a food but signals the anagram of RELIES ON.
explanation.definitionFit: The castle where Hamlet is set is in Denmark, a Shakespeare play's location.

clue.text: Withdraw article in reject

indicators.note: the article is placed inside the word for reject

parts.note: to repel something is to reject or drive it back
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A request to take back an item in a refused batch.
explanation.definitionFit: Revoking a law is to withdraw it officially.

clue.text: Criticism covers argument for covert weapon

indicators.note: the criticism wraps around the argument, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: stick is informal for criticism, as in giving someone stick
words, as in having words, means an argument

explanation.surface: Harsh comments conceal a quarrel about a hidden blade.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'give someone stick' is British slang for criticising them, and to 'have words' is to argue.
explanation.definitionFit: A cane concealing a blade is a hidden arm.

clue.text: Vehicle currently parking in a bog

indicators.note: the two short pieces sit inside the word for a bog

parts.note: a slough is a muddy bog
now means currently
P is the map symbol for parking

explanation.surface: A car park is now a swamp, it seems, with a vehicle stuck.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine for clearing snowy roads is a kind of truck or vehicle.

clue.text: Israel admits demand for vegetable

indicators.note: Israel lets the demand in, so it goes inside

parts.note: Sion, also spelt Zion, stands for Israel
a call is a demand, as in a call on resources

explanation.surface: Israel lets in a call for green onions.
explanation.definitionFit: A spring onion is a vegetable.

clue.text: Out of place in leisure clothes?

explanation.surface: Someone looks wrong without formal dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Being unsuitable is inappropriate; read literally it means not wearing a suit, as in casual wear.

clue.text: Hang on! That's underwear!

parts.note: to linger is to hang on or stay
i.e. stands for id est, that is

explanation.surface: Wait a moment: those are someone's undies!
explanation.definitionFit: Women's intimate garments are underwear.

clue.text: A length of time in a resort

indicators.note: the period of time goes inside the word for the resort

parts.note: a centre is a place people resort to, a hub of activity
taken as written

explanation.surface: Measuring how long you spend at a seaside holiday town.
explanation.definitionFit: A hundredth of a metre is a unit of length.

clue.text: Endlessly joining plant polymer

indicators.note: with no ends, the word for joining loses its first and last letters

parts.note: aligning can mean joining up with, allying

explanation.surface: An eternal bonding of a substance in plants.
explanation.definitionFit: The woody substance stiffening plant cell walls is a complex polymer.

clue.text: Doctor in storm hazard

indicators.note: the doctor sits inside the storm

parts.note: a gale is a storm
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: A medic caught out in a dangerous storm.
explanation.definitionFit: To hazard is to risk or bet something.

clue.text: The French slip up and accelerate suddenly

parts.note: le is French for the
to trip is to slip up or stumble

explanation.surface: A Frenchman stumbles and then dashes off.
explanation.definitionFit: To speed up all at once is to let fly, an idiom for going fast.

clue.text: Desire to embrace posh oriental and lie around

indicators.note: the desire wraps around the posh letter

parts.note: to long is to desire
U means upper class, posh
E is east, oriental

explanation.surface: A wish to hug a classy Easterner and then laze about.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper class, posh, comes from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U usage.
explanation.definitionFit: To loll idly is to lie about doing nothing.

clue.text: Don't drop one's aitches like Captain 'ook, for example

parts.note: as means like
Captain Hook of Peter Pan is a pirate; the apostrophe drops his H

explanation.surface: Cockney Captain Hook, without his H, is told to pronounce it properly.
explanation.walkthrough: Ironically, ''ook' has dropped its H, showing what the definition tells you not to do.
explanation.definitionFit: To breathe out an H sound is to sound the letter, the phonetic term.

clue.text: Detain for an endless period in the pub

indicators.note: the shortened period goes inside the word for the pub

parts.note: an inn is a pub

indicators.note: the period loses its last letter

parts.note: a term is a period of time

explanation.surface: Keep someone at the bar for ages.
explanation.definitionFit: To confine someone in wartime, or hold them without trial, is to detain them.

clue.text: Mineral a Roman patrician has to ban

parts.note: Cinna was a patrician family name of ancient Rome
to bar is to ban

explanation.surface: A Roman noble is forced to prohibit something.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercury sulphide, the red ore of mercury, is a mineral.

clue.text: Eccentric is to be introduced to Edward. Agreed?

indicators.note: the eccentric goes into the name, put inside it

parts.note: Ned is a pet form of Edward
odd means eccentric

explanation.surface: An oddball is about to meet Edward; is that settled?
explanation.definitionFit: To bob your head is a gesture of assent, of agreeing.

clue.text: Weep about family daughter being superficial

indicators.note: the weep word wraps around the family and daughter

parts.note: to seep is to ooze or weep
kin means family
D is daughter in genealogies

explanation.surface: Crying over a family girl who is shallow.
explanation.definitionFit: Something only on the surface, not going deeper, is superficial.
